name: Sugaring paste

lead: Sugaring paste is a sticky mixture, traditionally of sugar, water and lemon juice, applied to the skin and pulled off to remove hair at the root. The payoff is smooth, hair-free skin for weeks on the body or face.

Proponents say the paste grips hair rather than skin, is water-soluble and can be used at room temperature or lightly warmed, and prefer it to wax. The medical literature classes sugaring as epilation, grouped with plucking, threading, waxing, lasers and electrolysis. No trials specifically compare sugaring with waxing.

paras: People spread or flick the paste against hair growth and pull it off with the grain, working in small patches. It is used on legs, underarms, face and pubic area, with results that last until hair regrows.
Skin irritation is possible, especially on sensitive skin. Reviews note limited evidence on risks and that studies mostly cover dark hair and fair skin. Some products sold as sugar wax contain wax.

angle.text: Sugar paste removes body and facial hair at the root, leaving smooth skin that is visible right after and lasts for weeks. Users prefer it as a gentler alternative to wax.

lead: Sugaring paste is a sticky mixture, traditionally of sugar, water and lemon juice, spread on the skin and pulled off to remove hair at the root. People use it to get smooth skin on the legs, underarms, face, bikini area and other places, with results that last for weeks, and it is marketed as an alternative to wax.[1][2] Medical literature classes sugaring as a form of epilation alongside plucking, threading, waxing, lasers and electrolysis.

Proponents say the paste grips hair rather than skin, can be used at room temperature or lightly warmed, rinses off with water, and allows another session after about 8 to 10 days of regrowth.[1] The Cleveland Clinic describes the paste as pulled in the direction of hair growth, which it says may break fewer hairs and irritate less than wax, and notes that smoothness typically lasts around three weeks.[2]

Sugaring is also reported as one of the methods used for pubic hair removal. Published research on hair removal covers the category in general, and no trials specifically compare sugaring with waxing.
infobox: Sugar, water, lemon juice; sometimes honey, cornstarch [1]
Hair ready again after 8 to 10 days [1]; smoothness about three weeks [2]
Offered at many salons; home kits sold [2]

paras: Home recipes typically combine sugar, water and lemon juice, with cornstarch, honey or molasses in some versions; the acid in the lemon breaks sucrose down into fructose and glucose, yielding a smooth non-crystalline paste.[1] Commercial pastes may add guar gum or essential oils, and some products sold as sugar waxes contain actual wax.[1] The Cleveland Clinic notes that kits are sold for home use while advising against homemade recipes.[2]

Wikipedia notes that most store-bought products contain wax, whereas homemade versions usually use sugar and natural ingredients, and that getting the consistency right takes practice. The paste is water-based, so it cleans up with warm water [1].

In the strip method, the skin is dusted with powder, paste is spread on in the direction of hair growth, and a cloth or paper strip is pressed in and pulled off. In the traditional hand method, a ball of paste is applied against hair growth and flicked off along it, without strips, and residue is rinsed away with water.[1] Hair needs to be at least a few millimeters long for either sugaring or waxing, and sugaring often takes several passes over the same area.[2]

The Cleveland Clinic describes a salon version in which the paste is warmed to about body temperature, applied to cleaned skin against the direction of hair growth and removed in quick flicks with the growth direction. It contrasts this with waxing, where wax goes on with the growth and is pulled against it, which the clinic says can snap hairs [2]. Waxing is often finished in one pass, whereas sugaring may take several passes; typical areas include arms, back, bikini area, face, legs and underarms [2].

The Wikipedia article says that strip sugaring allows hair removal again after 8 to 10 days of growth, compared with 3 to 4 weeks for traditional waxing, while Cleveland Clinic gives about three weeks for sugaring results and two to eight weeks for waxing depending on hair growth speed [1][2].

Wikipedia states the method dates to about 1900 BC and was long confined to the region around Persia until the first millennium AD, with honey possibly the earliest sugaring agent. It is known by regional names including sukkar or halawa in the Middle East, agda in Turkey and moum in Iran.[1]
Wikipedia's article carries maintenance tags noting missing citations in places, and its history covers only the 1900 BC claim and the regional names [1].

sections.h: Sugaring compared with other hair-removal methods
paras: A literature review of hair removal practices classes sugaring with plucking, threading and waxing as epilation: the hair is pulled out with its root, so regrowth is typically slower than after shaving. All methods other than electrolysis are described as temporary. Laser and light-based methods and electrolysis aim for longer-lasting reduction and are performed by trained operators, while sugaring is available at salons and as home kits [2].

Wikipedia states that because the paste adheres to hair rather than skin it is less painful than waxing and is generally preferred for larger areas, and that sugar is hypoallergenic, although sensitive skin may still react [1]. Cleveland Clinic says some people find it less painful but that tolerance varies, and that it removes fewer surface skin cells than wax and typically causes less irritation [2].

Wikipedia's waxing article describes soft strip waxing, in which wax is spread and a strip is pulled against hair growth, and stripless hard wax that is removed once it sets, and says results last about two to eight weeks, with ingrown hairs, red bumps and minor bleeding among the drawbacks. It lists conditions that make skin lifting more likely, including topical retinoids, steroids, blood thinners, recent sunburn and rosacea. [3] Sugaring and waxing therefore share the same mechanism of pulling hair out at the root and overlap in many of their cautions.

Proponents report less pain than waxing, easier cleanup, lower burn risk because the paste can be used at room temperature, and a shorter wait between sessions.[1] The Cleveland Clinic lists less skin irritation, easy cleanup and possibly softer, thinner regrowth with repeated treatments, and notes that pain tolerance varies.[2] A dermatologist quoted by Cleveland Clinic said every method has pros and cons depending on the person, area, skin type and budget.[2]

A literature review found that most studies of hair removal methods are restricted to darker hair and fairer skin and that all methods besides electrolysis are temporary, each with its own advantages and adverse events.

Irritation or allergic reaction can occur on sensitive skin.[1] Cleveland Clinic lists irritation, inflammation, ingrown hairs (more likely with coarse, curly hair and in skin folds) and sore spots from skin-cell removal as possible effects, and says people who have taken isotretinoin should wait at least six months, and that sunburned, inflamed or infected skin and irritating topicals such as tretinoin are reasons to hold off.[2] A dermatological review of genital hair removal found little evidence on risks for methods such as sugaring.

Cleveland Clinic lists people who should avoid sugaring or take care: those with sunburned, inflamed or infected skin, eczema, very sensitive skin or skin that darkens with irritation, and users of tretinoin, who it says should stop a few days beforehand. It advises avoiding sun exposure before and after treatment, and avoiding scrubs, oils and friction for a few days afterward [2]. It recommends against homemade recipes and suggests checking salon reviews and sanitation practices [2].

No studies found specific to sugaring paste. Broader reviews of hair removal practices list sugaring among epilation methods without separate efficacy data. The Wikipedia article cites a 2018 study of pubic hair removal among Saudi women when discussing complications [1]. A dermatological review of genital hair removal describes motivations, methods and risks across methods and found little evidence specific to sugaring.

lore.intro: Sugaring is discussed in beauty and body-hair communities as a gentler alternative to waxing, with salon and home-kit versions both in circulation. [1][2]

claims.claim: Pulling with the direction of hair growth breaks fewer hairs
Sugaring causes less skin irritation than wax
Sugaring paste is natural and hypoallergenic
Repeated sugaring leads to softer, finer regrowth
Sugaring allows treatment again sooner than waxing

timeline.event: Date Wikipedia gives for the origin of sugaring as a hair-removal method.[1]
Sugar use said to spread beyond the region around Persia; honey speculated as the earliest agent [1].
Tannir and Leshin publish a Dermatologic Surgery article on sugaring as an ancient hair-removal method, later cited by Wikipedia [1].
Fernandez and colleagues publish a timeline of hair-removal methods in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology, cited by Wikipedia [1].
A BMC Women's Health study of pubic hair removal among Saudi women is cited by Wikipedia in discussing complications [1].
Skin Therapy Letter publishes a literature review of hair removal practices that classes sugaring as epilation.
JDDG publishes a dermatological review of genital hair removal motivation, methods and risks.
